Nonhealing sore on right foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
The patient presents for evaluation of a right foot wound present for approximately 2–3 weeks. He reports no specific trauma. He denies pain (“can’t feel it”), fever, chills, or drainage, though he notes his sock sometimes sticks to the wound even when covered with a bandage. He has a history of stability issues at times. ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right lateral/dorsal forefoot near 5th MTP, nonhealing 
Assessment: Nonhealing ulcer for 2–3 weeks following shoe-related pressure/friction in the setting of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Exam today notable for a ~1 x 2 inch circular wound with yellow slough and minimal granulation tissue; no surrounding erythema or cellulitis, no odor, no necrosis, no fluctuance, and no exposed bone. - Start collagenase ointment once daily; cover with a dry sterile dressing. Continue until wound is shrinking and healthy pink granulation tissue is present. 
- Offloading: Wear a surgical shoe to take pressure off the area; avoid the prior tight footwear. 
- No further antibiotics at this time given lack of clinical infection. 
- Order ankle-brachial index (ABI) to assess perfusion and healing potential. Refer to vascular specialist if ABI indicates suboptimal blood supply. 
- Return to clinic in 2 weeks for wound reassessment, sooner if increasing pain, redness, swelling, drainage, malodor, fever, or spreading erythema.

Assessment: Suboptimal glycemic control likely impairing wound healing. 
Plan: 
- Emphasize importance of improved glycemic control to facilitate wound healing. 
- Consider diabetes consult for additional dietary counseling and management strategies to reduce A1c.

Follow-up instructions: 
- Follow up in 2 weeks for wound check, or sooner for any signs of infection or worsening wound. 
- Proceed with ABI as ordered; potential vascular referral based on results. 
- Use surgical shoe consistently and apply collagenase with daily dressing changes as instructed.

["SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Emergency room follow-up after hyperglycemia. 
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Albert is a 62-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes, depression, and kidney transplant, presenting for ER follow-up. Over the weekend he felt “woozy” and was found to have high blood sugars in the ER; he was not admitted. He attributes the elevation to dietary indiscretion and poor monitoring while his mother was hospitalized (cafeteria/fast food). He felt better after the ER visit and reports closer adherence to diet since. Typically his diet is good during the week but less consistent on weekends due to social activities. He reports good adherence to his immunosuppression; he saw Dr. Reyes (transplant nephrology) about 3 weeks ago and was told kidney function is good. Regarding mood, he notes the past 1.5 years have been challenging but he is coping; meditation has been helpful and he prefers to avoid medications or therapy at this time. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or dizziness. 

"ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus with recent hyperglycemia, suboptimally controlled 
Assessment: Recent ER visit for symptomatic hyperglycemia related to dietary lapse. In-clinic glucose 162 mg/dL (patient had not eaten) and hemoglobin A1c 8%, indicating elevated average glucose over the past months. 
Plan: 
- Increase insulin glargine (Lantus) to 20 units nightly. 
- Continue home blood glucose monitoring and report trends to the clinic for potential further titration. 
- Order repeat hemoglobin A1c in a couple of months. 

2. Depression, stable without pharmacotherapy 
Assessment: Patient reports coping with intermittent low mood; meditation and relaxation are helpful. He prefers to avoid medications and formal therapy currently. 
Plan: 
- Continue meditation and current coping strategies. 
- Hold off on medication or therapy at this time; patient will call if needs arise. 

3. Status post kidney transplant, stable graft function 
Assessment: Adherent to immunosuppression; saw Dr. Reyes ~3 weeks ago with stable kidney function. 
Plan: 
- Continue immunosuppression as prescribed. 
- Ongoing management of immunosuppression through Dr. Reyes; he will reach out if coordination is needed. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- Monitor and share home blood glucose readings for dose adjustment as needed. 
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in a couple of months. 
- Contact the clinic if mood worsens or if hyperglycemia symptoms recur.]

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient presents with left knee pain after twisting the knee while running with her 5-year-old niece about one week ago as the niece was learning to ride a bike without training wheels. She heard a “pop” at the time of injury. Since then she has been able to bear weight but has been limping, and the pain has been worsening. Pain is throbbing, located on both sides of the knee, worse medially. She reports swelling. She cannot take NSAIDs due to a recent ulcer and has been using acetaminophen, which provides only brief relief; she is aware not to take it too frequently. She applied kinesiology tape.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Left knee injury—suspected medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain
Assessment: Twisting mechanism with medial-predominant pain and tenderness, edema/effusion, limited range of motion with pain on flexion/extension. Stability testing negative (Lachman, varus/valgus), and left knee x-ray today shows no fracture or bony abnormality. Overall consistent with MCL strain rather than ligament tear.
Plan:
- Pain control: Start tramadol 50 mg twice daily. May use acetaminophen as needed for breakthrough pain; avoid exceeding recommended dosing.
- Immobilization: Knee immobilizer for 1 week to limit motion and reduce inflammation.
- Ice: Apply 3–4 times daily for 20–30 minutes each session.
- Activity: Avoid running for the next 3 weeks.
- Imaging/contingency: If symptoms worsen or fail to improve, contact the office; consider MRI to evaluate for internal derangement if clinical course is not improving.

2. History of recent ulcer—analgesic considerations
Assessment: Contraindication to NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen/Advil) due to recent ulcer.
Plan:
- Avoid NSAIDs.
- Use non-NSAID regimen as above (tramadol with PRN acetaminophen), with caution about acetaminophen overuse.

Follow-up instructions:
- Expect gradual improvement and return to normal activity in about 1 month if adhering to the plan.
- Update the office in a couple of days on progress, and call sooner for worsening pain, swelling, or new instability; MRI may be pursued if not improving.
